title: Joshua's Final Call to Choose
overview: At the end of his life Joshua gathers Israel, retells what God has done for them, and asks them to commit to serving the LORD alone, which they solemnly promise.

parts.label: Gathering at Shechem (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Joshua calls the leaders to Shechem, the place where Abraham first stopped in Canaan and where Jacob once buried his family's idols under an oak. Speaking as God's messenger, he begins with Abraham's family, who worshiped other gods until God called Abraham away.

parts.label: From Egypt to the land (vv. 5-13)
parts.note: The speech retells the escape from Egypt, the desert years, the wars on both sides of the Jordan, and Balaam, a hired seer whose curse kept turning into blessing, to stress that the land, its cities and its vineyards were a gift rather than something Israel earned. It plainly credits God with driving out the people already living there, and whether the 'hornet' means real swarms or a picture of sudden panic is unclear.

parts.label: Choose whom you serve (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Joshua urges them to get rid of the gods their ancestors worshiped in Mesopotamia and Egypt and serve the LORD with honest hearts. He presents it as a real choice, while stating that he and his household have already made theirs.

parts.label: A pledge and a hard warning (vv. 16-24)
parts.note: The people eagerly promise loyalty, but Joshua replies that they cannot keep it, because God is holy and will not shrug off them turning to other gods. Many read this as a deliberate jolt to make them weigh the promise, and they repeat it three times anyway.

parts.label: The agreement and the stone (vv. 25-28)
parts.note: Joshua makes the agreement official that day, writes it down, and sets up a large stone under an oak, a common ancient way to mark a public pact. The stone is pictured as a witness that 'heard' every word and would stand there as a reminder if they broke faith.

parts.label: Three burials (vv. 29-33)
parts.note: Joshua dies at 110, the priest Eleazar dies too, and Joseph's bones, carried out of Egypt at his own dying request, are finally buried at Shechem on land Jacob had bought. The remark that Israel stayed faithful while Joshua's generation lived quietly sets up the drifting away told in the next book, Judges.

think: Joshua roots a present commitment in a remembered past; which stories from your own history most shape what you choose to give yourself to?
